But your eyes were fixed, unwilling to yield.
As we moved forward, I couldn't help but feel a pang of curiosity.
You, with your rugged exterior and weathered face, were a man who seemed to have seen the world and its hardships.
Yet, there was a softness in your gaze, a gentleness that was as unexpected as it was captivating.
Over the years, I had heard stories about you.
Stories of bravery, of selflessness, and of resilience.
How you single-handedly saved a family from a burning building, or how you risked your life to rescue a child from a flooded ravine.
Each tale was more incredible than the last, and they all seemed to paint a picture of a hero.
But you, you always downplayed it.
You'd brush off the compliments, insisting that you were just doing what anyone else would have done.
You'd change the subject, avoid the spotlight, and shrug off the accolades that were bestowed upon you.
So, when that little girl, her eyes wide with wonder, called out to you, "Hero!" as you walked past her on the street, I wasn't surprised by your reaction.

Five rounds left. Not enough, but it would have to do.

blocks.text: "He heard the shouting before he saw them coming.
The deafening roar of the crowd, the clashing of weapons, and the primal screams echoed through the vast expanse of his domain.
God took one look out the window and groaned.
He reached for his aspirin - it had earned a spot in every room he owned - and plodded downstairs to the foyer.
The smell of fresh blood, sweat, and fear wafted up to his nostrils as he opened the door.
Down in the arena, his creatures, the pinnacle of his creation, were locked in a brutal battle.
They were the apotheosis of natural selection, honed by countless millennia to be the ultimate killing machines.
He had created them for one purpose: to fight and win in gladiatorial tournaments against other deities' creations.
Each one was a masterpiece of brutality, their bodies sculpted to withstand the most gruesome of attacks, their minds honed to outsmart and outmaneuver their opponents.
Yet, as he looked upon them, a feeling of sadness washed over him.
For in this pursuit of perfection, he had forgotten what it meant to create beings that could love, feel empathy, and understand compassion.
He walked down the steps, his heavy footsteps echoing through the silent night.
The crowd fell silent as he descended, their eyes following him.
He reached the pit, his gaze fixed on the two combatants.
One of his, the other, a creation of a rival deity.
The air was thick with tension, the seconds ticking by excruciatingly slow.
And then, with a sudden burst of energy, the combatants lunged at each other.

blocks.text: (First timer here, be gentle! Sorry it's a little long.)
I'm still not certain exactly how it happened, but to be honest, I'm okay with that.
All I know is that one minute I was driving home after a long day at work, and the next, I found myself in a small, dimly lit café.
The room was filled with an odd assortment of individuals, each engrossed in their own world, save for one.
At a table by the window, Death was sitting with his back towards me.
His silhouette was unmistakable, despite the shadows.
I hesitated, unsure if I should approach, but curiosity got the better of me.
As I moved closer, he turned to face me, and my breath caught in my throat.
Death extended a hand, gesturing for me to sit.
I hesitated, still stunned, but he merely raised an eyebrow, as if to say that there was no going back.
I hesitated for a moment longer before I sat across from him.
The silence between us grew heavy, and I nervously fiddled with the fraying hem of my shirt.
Death, however, seemed to be in no rush.
He picked up his coffee, and I watched as he added an absurd amount of creamer.
"I find it helps to sweeten the taste," he said, meeting my gaze.
"Life can be quite bitter, after all." I couldn't help but think of the countless cups of coffee I'd drunk in my life, the comfort they'd provided during stressful times.
I realized then that maybe death wasn't so different.
It was simply another part of life, a bitter pill to swallow, but one that could be made more palatable if approached with the right attitude.

The package, oddly sent through a private courier, felt heavy as I picked it up from the mailbox.
The return address read: 'From the Other Side, c/o Time and Space.', and the stamp bore an eerie resemblance to none I've ever seen.
Inside the box, I find a worn, leather-bound journal, its pages yellowed and brittle.
The first few pages contain my brother's handwriting, fading and shaky, just like the letter.

I've seen the hardships you've faced and the strength you've shown.

blocks.text: "We done here?" I asked exasperatedly, leaning against the cold metallic wall of the lab.
The man in the lab coat looked up, a bit apologetically, "just one more test for the day, please." I rolled my eyes and sighed, running a hand through my messy hair.
"I've been bouncing around like a ping-pong ball all day," I complained, "and for what?
So they can study this 'double-jump' thing?

It's just a simple ability, not a cure for cancer or anything." The man in the lab coat, Dr. Chen, gave me a gentle smile, "I understand your frustration, but this ability could potentially revolutionize human movement and physics.
You are a trailblazer, and your contributions are invaluable." I sighed and pushed myself off the wall, "fine, just one more test.
But after this, I'm heading home to my bed and my video games." Dr. Chen nodded and pointed to a series of markers on the floor, "this time, we're measuring your jumping height and distance.
Remember, try to jump as high and as far as you can." I rolled my eyes again but nodded, taking a deep breath and focusing on the task at hand.
I jumped, soared through the air, and landed gracefully on the cushioned mat Dr. Chen had prepared.
I repeated this several times, each jump higher and farther than the last.
After what felt like hours, Dr. Chen signaled for me to stop, "that will be enough for today.
You've done an excellent job, thank you." I gave him a tired smile, "no problem.
I'll see you tomorrow." As I left the lab, I couldn't help but feel a sense of pride.

blocks.text: I remember my first days as a doctor.
I wore my stethoscope proudly around my neck, not realizing it advertised how much of a virgin I was in the field of medicine.
I'd introduce myself as Dr. Agon and tried to project confidence, masking the nervousness that bubbled within me.
I was determined to make a difference, to heal and save lives.
But years passed, and the weight of responsibility grew heavier.
The system I once admired for its ethics and compassion began to reveal its flaws.
I saw patients neglected, their cries for help falling on deaf ears due to bureaucratic red tape.
I witnessed the corruption that permeated the system, and I found myself growing disillusioned.
I started to question my role, my purpose.
I began to see myself as a mere cog in a flawed machine, unable to effect meaningful change.
And in that moment of despair, I made a fateful decision.
I would no longer be a silent observer, a helpless bystander.
I would become a hero, but not the kind that adheres to the rules and moral compass of society.
I would become a hero who bent them to his will.
I used my knowledge and position to manipulate the system, to get what I wanted, to help who I wanted.
I became a ghost in the hospital, a phantom doctor who worked in the shadows.
I was no longer the idealistic, young Dr. Agon, but a villain in my own story.
I reveled in the power, the control, the freedom.
But as I watched the line between right and wrong blur, I began to realize the cost of my actions.
I saw the fear in the eyes of the patients I had once sworn to protect.
